transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Um, yeah, so I made this appointment because, well, it’s just been getting really frustrating lately. The main reason I came in is that I just get pulled off track so easily. Like, unbelievably easily. 

I’ll be sitting at my desk, right? And I’m trying to work on this data dashboard I’m supposed to be finishing for my program—which is already taking forever because the formatting is super tedious and you have to double-check all the inputs—but anyway, I'll be right in the middle of it, and then just one single Slack ping goes off on my laptop from a group project chat. Or honestly, not even that, sometimes it’s just a random song lyric that pops into my head out of nowhere, or I’ll suddenly get this entirely new, completely unrelated idea for another project that I'm not even supposed to be thinking about right now. 

And before I even realize what I'm doing, I've opened like twelve new tabs, I'm looking up domain names for that random project idea, or I'm trying to find the exact album that song is from, and suddenly I’ve completely lost the thread of the dashboard I was supposed to be finishing. It's like my brain just completely drops whatever is actually important the second something else pops up, and then hours go by and I'm like, wait, what was I even doing? It just happens all the time, every single day, and I really need to figure out how to stop doing it because I just can't seem to stay on one train of thought.
Has this difficulty staying focused been an issue for you since childhood, or is it something that started more recently?

Oh, it’s definitely been since childhood. Like, pretty much as long as I can remember, honestly. I actually was just looking at some of my old report cards recently because my mom keeps them all in this huge binder at home, and it’s kind of funny, well, not funny, but just really telling, because even way back in elementary school, my teachers were writing the exact same things. 

They would always leave these long comments about how I was rushing through my worksheets. I’d just speed through them because I wanted to be done, and I’d make all these careless mistakes. And they were always saying I was losing track of directions. Like, the teacher would give us a three-step instruction for a project, and by the time I finished step one, I had completely forgotten what step two and three were, or I was already doing something else entirely. And group work was... oh my gosh, group work was always a huge issue. The teachers constantly wrote that I was talking over my classmates. It wasn’t that I was trying to be rude or anything, I just... I’d get so excited about a thought, or I’d be so worried I was going to forget what I wanted to say, that I would just blurt it out right in the middle of someone else speaking. I still feel kind of bad about that, actually. 

And then at home, homework was just a complete nightmare for everyone involved. My parents literally had to sit right beside me at the kitchen table every single night. Like, physically sit next to me the entire time. Because if they didn't, if they just got up to check the oven or went into the other room for two minutes, I would completely wander off. I’d go to get a pencil and end up playing with the dog, or I’d start a completely different assignment before I even finished the first one, or I'd just be staring at the wall daydreaming. So they basically had to act like my personal guards just to get me through a basic spelling worksheet. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing at all, it’s always been exactly like this, it's just that now I'm in college and my parents aren't here to sit next to me while I do my data dashboards, you know?
Do you often feel physically restless or find yourself constantly fidgeting and having trouble sitting still?

Oh, yeah. Definitely. I mean, it’s honestly kind of embarrassing because I literally cannot just sit like a normal person. Like, if I'm in a meeting for a group project, or, oh, especially during my portfolio reviews for my major—which are already super stressful because you have all the professors just staring at your work and judging it—I am almost always doing something physical. 

I’ll be sitting there bouncing my leg, and sometimes I bounce it so hard that the actual table starts shaking, which is just awful when other people have their laptops on it. Or I’ll be sitting there clicking my pen over and over, just clicking it without even thinking, or twisting my rings around my fingers. I actually wear a lot of rings specifically because I like the way they feel, but they kind of clink together when I twist them, so it makes this tiny metallic noise. And I’m constantly shifting around in my chair, too, like I'm trying to find a comfortable position but I never actually find one, so I just keep crossing and uncrossing my legs. 

The worst part is that I don’t even really notice I’m doing any of it. I'll just be completely focused on trying to listen to the critique, twisting my rings or shaking the table with my leg, and I won't realize it until someone finally looks at me. You know that look? Like they just glance down at my bouncing leg or stare at my hands with this slightly annoyed expression, and then suddenly I’m hyper-aware of it and I force myself to freeze and sit perfectly still. But then, like, two minutes later, I’m doing it again without even realizing. I just have this constant, buzzing need to be moving some part of my body, even if it's just a tiny movement, otherwise I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin. My friends always joke that I have a motor attached to me, but it's really not funny when you're in a quiet room and you're the only one making noise with a pen, you know? It's just so hard to just... exist in a chair.
